questions.q: What is the name given to the amount of magnetic field passing through a given area, and what is its SI unit?
options: Magnetic flux density, measured in tesla (T)
Magnetic flux, symbol \(\phi_B\), measured in weber (Wb)
Magnetic field strength, measured in newtons (N)
Magnetic permeability, measured in weber per square metre (Wb m\(^{-2}\))
questions.explanation: Magnetic flux is the name given to the amount of magnetic field passing through a given area. It is given the symbol \(\phi_B\) and in the SI system is measured in weber (Wb). Tesla is the unit of magnetic field strength (flux density), not of flux.

questions.q: The strength of a magnetic field, B, is also known as the magnetic flux density. In which units is the magnetic flux density measured?
options: weber (Wb) only
tesla (T), or equivalently weber per square metre (Wb m\(^{-2}\))
weber per second (Wb s\(^{-1}\))
newton per ampere-metre (N A\(^{-1}\) m\(^{-1}\)) only
questions.explanation: The strength of a magnetic field, B, is also known as the magnetic flux density — the amount of magnetic flux passing through a unit area. In the SI system, B is measured in tesla (T) or weber per square metre (Wb m\(^{-2}\)), which makes the 'per unit area' meaning of density explicit.

questions.q: From memory: state the relationship between magnetic flux, magnetic flux density and area when the area A is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of strength B, and state what happens to the flux when the field is parallel to the area.
keyPoints: If the area A is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of strength B, the magnetic flux \(\phi_B\) is the product of B and A: \(\phi_B = BA\).
More generally \(\phi_B = B_\perp A\), where \(B_\perp\) is the component of the magnetic flux density perpendicular to the area.
The magnetic flux passing through an area is reduced if the field is not perpendicular to the area, and \(\phi_B\) is zero if the magnetic field is parallel to the area.
questions.explanation: When the area is perpendicular to the field, \(\phi_B = BA\) (every field line threads the area). When the field is parallel to the area it skims across and \(\phi_B = 0\). If you recalled \(\phi_B = BA\) and the zero-when-parallel case, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: The syllabus relationship for describing how magnetic flux can change is written \(\phi = B_\parallel A = BA\cos\theta\). In this relationship, what does the factor \(\cos\theta\) account for?
options: The number of turns in the coil
The orientation of the field relative to the area, so only the component of the flux density passing through the area contributes
The rate at which the flux changes with time
The conversion between tesla and weber
questions.explanation: The relationship \(\phi = B_\parallel A = BA\cos\theta\) describes how magnetic flux depends on orientation. Magnetic flux through an area is the product of the area and the component of the magnetic flux density passing through it; \(\cos\theta\) extracts that component, giving maximum flux when the field passes straight through and zero when it is parallel to the area.

questions.q: Calculate the magnetic flux threading an area of 1.5 m\(^2\) that is perpendicular to a magnetic field of flux density 2.0 T.
questions.given: \(A = 1.5\,\mathrm{m^2}\), flux density \(B = 2.0\,\mathrm{T}\), area perpendicular to the field so \(\theta = 0\)
working: The area is perpendicular to the field, so \(\theta = 0\) and \(\cos\theta = 1\): \(\phi_B = BA\)
questions.explanation: With the area perpendicular to the field, \(\theta = 0\) and \(\phi_B = BA = 2.0 \times 1.5 = 3.0\,\mathrm{Wb}\). Flux is in webers, not tesla — an answer 'in tesla' would signal you had found a field strength instead.

questions.q: Calculate the magnetic flux threading a rectangle with a length of 4.0 cm and width 3.0 cm that is perpendicular to a magnetic field of flux density \(5.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{T}\).
questions.given: rectangle \(0.040\,\mathrm{m} \times 0.030\,\mathrm{m}\), flux density \(B = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{T}\), area perpendicular to the field so \(\theta = 0\)
working: Convert to metres and find the area: \(A = 0.040 \times 0.030 = 1.2 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2}\)
questions.explanation: Convert centimetres to metres before multiplying: \(A = 1.2 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2}\). With the rectangle perpendicular to the field, \(\phi_B = BA = 6.0 \times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{Wb}\).

questions.q: Define the concept of magnetic flux in terms of magnetic flux density and surface area. (2 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: Magnetic flux \(\phi_B\) is the amount of magnetic field passing through a given area. It is the product of the area, A, and the component of the magnetic flux density, B, that is perpendicular to that area: \(\phi_B = B_\perp A = BA\cos\theta\). It is measured in weber (Wb), whereas the flux density B is measured in tesla.

criteria.descriptor: States magnetic flux is the amount of magnetic field (the perpendicular flux density) passing through a given area.
Gives the relationship \(\phi_B = BA\) (or \(B_\perp A\)) linking flux to flux density and surface area, with unit weber.

questions.explanation: The marks reward defining flux as flux density times area (the perpendicular component) and specifying the surface area — flux is meaningless without a stated area.

questions.q: In the flux equation \(\phi = BA\cos\theta\) as taught in this episode, the angle \(\theta\) is measured from which reference?
options: Between the magnetic field and the plane of the loop
Between the magnetic field and the area vector (the normal — the direction perpendicular to the plane of the loop)
Between the area vector and the plane of the loop
Between two adjacent magnetic field lines
questions.explanation: The episode stresses that \(\theta\) is the angle between the magnetic field and the area vector (the normal to the loop), not the angle to the plane of the loop. Measuring from the plane instead of the normal is the single most common flux error in the HSC.

questions.q: From memory: as a coil rotates steadily in a uniform magnetic field, explain why the flux through it changes continuously, and state at which orientations the flux is maximum and zero.
keyPoints: B and A stay constant, but the angle \(\theta\) between the field and the coil's area vector changes continuously, so \(\phi = BA\cos\theta\) changes continuously.
Flux is maximum (\(\phi = BA\)) when the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field — area vector aligned with the field, \(\theta = 0\), all field lines thread the coil.
Flux is zero when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field — area vector perpendicular to the field, \(\theta = 90^\circ\), field lines skim across without passing through.
questions.explanation: Use the window-in-the-rain image: window flat to the rain catches the most (max flux), edge-on catches none (zero flux). If you tied both orientations to \(\theta\) and the area vector, grade Good or Easy.

questions.q: A coil sits stationary in a strong, steady magnetic field, so there is a large flux through it. Is an emf induced in the coil?
options: Yes — a large flux always induces an emf
No — the flux is large but not changing, and only a change in flux induces an emf, not the flux itself
Yes — but only because the field is strong
No — because a stationary coil cannot carry any flux
questions.explanation: Although the flux is large, it is steady, and only a changing flux induces an emf. A big, unchanging flux does nothing on its own — the emf comes from the rate of change of flux (Faraday's law), which is the next episode. This is the central trap the episode guards against.
